$comment: Every place this port's classes differ from shadcn/ui, and why.
Read by BOTH tools/sync_classes.py (which writes the components) and the parity tests
(which check them), so the generator and the test can never disagree about what counts as
a deviation. Anything not listed here must match shadcn exactly, and the test fails if it
does not.
Adding an entry is a decision someone reviews. If the reason does not fit in a sentence,
the component is wrong, not the list.
Two kinds of substitution, and only two.
shadcn hardcodes the control height and font size, which pins every consumer to one control
size; h-control and text-control read --control-h and --control-text so one library can dress
a 46px storefront and a 36px back office.
And Radix draws a checkbox, a radio and a switch as a <button> carrying data-state, with a
hidden input alongside. Here the real input IS the control, because on static SSR it is the
only thing that posts and the only thing that can be focused — so the state lives in :checked,
which the browser maintains, rather than in an attribute JavaScript would have to keep in step.
Without this substitution those classes match nothing and the checked state has no colour at
Without this substitution those classes match nothing and the checked state has no colour at
all: the bug that shipped, and the reason each one is written down here.
A token name is matched wherever it appears, so it must be a name that can only ever mean the
substitution. `bg-input` was tried and was wrong for exactly that reason — every component
that legitimately says bg-input had it cancelled on one side of the comparison only.

avatar-image.why: Radix swaps image for fallback in JS after the load event. Here the fallback sits behind the image and the image hides itself on error, so the exchange costs no script and survives a fragment swap — which needs the image stacked above it. rounded-full is the other half of dropping overflow-hidden from the root: with the root no longer clipping, the image has to round itself or a square photo stays square.

avatar-fallback.why: It sits behind the image rather than replacing it, so the exchange costs no script and survives a fragment swap; see avatar-image. text-xs and font-medium were also here and were a hand-written leftover — they overrode upstream's own text-sm, which only tailwind-merge made visible.

dropdown-menu.why: Radix renders the menu through a portal, so its root needs no positioning. ui.js measures the trigger in place, so the root is the positioning context.

dropdown-menu-sub.why: Radix nests submenus through a portal. The popover API does not nest, so ui.js opens the child popover from the parent row and this element is the positioning context.

popover.why: Radix renders the panel through a portal, so its root needs no positioning. ui.js measures the trigger in place, so the root is the positioning context.

context-menu.why: The trigger and its panel need a common ancestor for the compiler to pair them, and upstream has none because React context does that job. Positioning only.

context-menu-sub.why: The trigger and its panel need a common ancestor for the compiler to pair them, and upstream has none because React context does that job. Positioning only.

menubar-menu.why: Upstream renders nothing here at all — it is a context provider. The trigger and the panel still need something holding them together for the compiler to find.

menubar-sub.why: Upstream renders nothing here at all — it is a context provider. The trigger and the panel still need something holding them together for the compiler to find.

combobox-content.why: Upstream draws the border and the stacking on a Popup primitive that has no slot of its own. In the top layer z-50 is inert, but the panel is styled the same either way and one class is cheaper than a second code path.

combobox-trigger.why: A combobox trigger shows a value, not a label: it fills its field, puts the chevron at the far end, and does not embolden what the user chose. Upstream gets all three from the call site, which a component cannot rely on.

combobox-trigger-icon.why: <Icon> ships shrink-0 on every icon, because an icon that shrinks inside a flex row is the single most common way one ends up an ellipse. Upstream writes it per call site instead.

combobox-item-indicator.why: <Icon> ships shrink-0 on every icon, because an icon that shrinks inside a flex row is the single most common way one ends up an ellipse. Upstream writes it per call site instead.

combobox-clear.why: Upstream ships no classes for it at all; an unstyled button here is browser chrome.

input-otp.why: Upstream splits this across two props: `className` dresses the real input and `containerClassName` dresses the box around it, and only the first carries the data-slot. Here the box IS the element, so it needs both — without them the six boxes were not in a row at all and wrapped onto two lines.

alert.why: AlertAction does not exist in the new-york-v4 source this port vendors, but shadcn documents it and the docs render it. Its geometry is taken from shadcn's own stylesheet — .cn-alert-action is absolute at the trailing top corner, and .cn-alert reserves the room with has-data-[slot=alert-action]:pr-18. pe- rather than pr-, so it swaps sides under dir="rtl".

carousel-next.why: An arrow glyph points along the reading direction. The button already moved to the end edge; the arrow inside it has to turn too, or "next" points back at the slide you came from. Only on the horizontal branch — a vertical carousel is rotated 90 degrees already and its direction has nothing to do with the writing direction.

sidebar-menu-sub.why: The hairline nudge that sits the list against its own border. The border is border-s now, so it is on the other edge under RTL and the nudge follows it. Tailwind has no logical translate, so this is the rtl: variant rather than a different utility.

bubble-reactions.why: The pill is rounded-full and has-[button]:p-0 lets a control fill it — but the control keeps the button recipe's rounded-md, so hovering painted a rounded SQUARE inside a circle. Nothing is wrong at rest, which is why it survived: it only shows under the pointer, and only on the two examples that put a control in a reaction slot.

attachment.why: Tailwind drops the whole candidate: a comma separates candidates in its parser, so `has-[>a,>button]:hover:bg-muted/50` compiles to NOTHING and emits no warning. The effect is that an attachment card carrying a trigger never tinted under the pointer — the one affordance that says the whole card is clickable — and it looked like the trigger was not there. Written as two candidates, which is the same selector twice.

dialog-content.why: A modal <dialog> is centred by the user agent and lives in the top layer, so the fixed positioning and z-index are the platform's job. Radix animates on data-state; <dialog> has [open], so the animation is a CSS rule in ui.behavior.css instead.

dropdown-menu-content.why: Those custom properties are set by Radix's positioning engine, which does not exist here — ui.js measures the anchor instead. The state animations go with them; the popover API exposes :popover-open, not data-state.

select-item.why: Radix's SelectItem is a div in a listbox. Here it is an <option> — the thing that actually posts, and the thing a phone renders as its own wheel. The OS draws it, so none of these classes reach anything. ui.js applies the same recipe to the themed row it draws beside the native control.

slider.why: Upstream's root is a <div> holding a track and a thumb, so it is a flex container. Here the root IS the <input type=range>, and display:flex on a range input destroys the box model the browser draws its own track and thumb inside — the track vanished and only the thumb was left, a lone circle floating in the row. The remaining layout classes (relative, w-full, touch-none, select-none) are harmless on an input and are kept.

combobox-trigger.why: Replaced by the two above; a value pinned to the middle in bold is not a value.

avatar.why: It clips the badge. AvatarBadge sits inside the root with ring-2 ring-background, and a rounded overflow-hidden parent cuts the ring off at the circle — the badge reads as a bitten crescent. shadcn's own docs do not show that, because the style they render (base) has no overflow-hidden on the root either: the circle comes from rounded-full on the image and the fallback, which is what this does now.

attachment.why: Tailwind drops the whole candidate: a comma separates candidates in its parser, so `has-[>a,>button]:hover:bg-muted/50` compiles to NOTHING and emits no warning. The effect is that an attachment card carrying a trigger never tinted under the pointer — the one affordance that says the whole card is clickable — and it looked like the trigger was not there. Written as two candidates, which is the same selector twice.

$comment: Components whose class-bearing element is not the first one they render, as component name
to the data-slot that carries the classes. Read by tools/sync_classes.py (which writes the
class list) and by the tests (which check it), so both always look at the same element.
Each entry exists because the platform needs a frame shadcn does not have.
Slots where shadcn wraps a Button with asChild, so the element carries the button recipe
rather than classes of its own. There is no cloneElement in Blazor, so the trigger IS the
button — and the expected classes are the button's, checked by the button parity tests.
Each entry names the button variant and size the component renders, so the comparison is
against the recipe it actually asks for rather than cva's default.
withSlotClasses says the slot ALSO carries classes of its own, which upstream passes as the
Button's className — so the expectation is the recipe followed by them, in that order,
because that is the order Button composes them in. Carousel's arrows need it: they override
the button's size and shape. Most do not, and dialog-close must not — upstream gives that
slot to two different elements, the corner X inside DialogContent and the Close a caller
puts in a footer, and this component is the second.
Components whose default rendering is not cva's default, keyed by component rather than by
slot — three components render pagination-link and two of them are not icon-sized.
shadcn passes these at the call site, where cva cannot see them.
Slots that render another component of this library, as upstream does. Its classes appear
in the output but belong to it, so the parity test subtracts them — and the generator must
NOT write them into the component, or they would land after the slot's own classes and win
the merge, which is exactly backwards.

input-group-control.component: Input or Textarea, whose own classes are checked on their own slots

sidebar-input.why: What <Input> brings, minus anything sidebar-input's own list repeats: subtracting a class the slot itself declares would take it off the rendered side only, and it would then read as missing.

$comment: Slots whose class list is a cva that carries no data-slot of its own. InputGroupButton
renders a <Button>, so in the DOM the element says data-slot="button" and its own size
table — the one that makes it small enough to sit inside a 36px control — belongs to no
slot at all. Without this it had no classes whatsoever and rendered as browser chrome
inside a styled box.
Components that render more than one classed element from a single call, as a C# const
per slot. Sidebar is the only one so far and it needs three: the group that carries the
state, a spacer that reserves the width in the document flow, and the fixed panel. The
spacer is what stops the page jumping when the panel collapses — the panel is fixed and
takes no space, so something has to hold it.
Slots rendered on a different HTML element than shadcn writes. Every one is a semantic
gain that costs nothing visually: shadcn reaches for a div because React makes the tag
the least interesting decision in the file, and static SSR has no such excuse.
element.attachment-group: a list of files is a <ul>; "list, 3 items" is how someone hears how many there are before deciding to go through them
element.avatar-group-count: "+3" sits inside a row of avatars, so it is a <span> — a div there would be a block box in an inline run
element.bubble: one turn in a conversation is an <article>, which is what lets a screen reader move between turns instead of reading the thread as one wall of text
element.message: the same, for the wider shape around a bubble
element.input-otp-slot: the slot IS the input here. Radix draws six divs and keeps the value in React with one hidden field behind them; on static SSR the six real inputs are what post, and what a password manager fills
